candidates.title: Harmonic Observatory
candidates.prompt:
Use case: ui-mockup. Create ONE gorgeous, believable high-fidelity desktop web application screenshot for the next version of "chord", a playable musical harmony explorer. Wide landscape 16:10 image, front-facing flat UI, edge to edge, no physical device, no browser chrome, no poster captions or external annotations.
Input image 1 is a reference screenshot of the CURRENT WORKING APPLICATION, not an exact edit target. Evolve its visual language and preserve recognizable keyboard/instrument usability, while substantially redesigning the main workspace.
Visual system: true black #000000 canvas, neutral charcoal #121212 surfaces, gray hairline separators, ivory text #e9e9e9. Cyan #74dce5, coral #f4b39b and violet #ac98e8 represent C, E and G and appear only in musical signals, active controls and selected notes. NO overall blue background tint. Proportional Manrope-like typography with excellent spacing, sentence-case labels, crisp readable text and thin consistent waveform/music icons. Not a generic dashboard; no analytics cards, fake percentages, decorative stars, rainbow gradients, glassmorphism, or huge bloom. Dense enough to be a real instrument, calm enough to let the main visualization dominate.
Common practical controls: small "chord" waveform wordmark; a concise view switch with "Overtones", "Tuning", "Chords", "Scope". One "Instrument / Pure tones" switch. At the bottom, a slim sound toolbar with "Sampled", "Synth", "Acoustic Grand Piano", one "Latch" control, "Stop", volume, octave controls; beneath it a real playable piano keyboard about 120px tall with repeating correct two-and-three black-key groups, small computer keyboard shortcut labels, C3 cyan, E3 coral, G3 violet. The visualization has separate "Freeze", "Follow sound" and "Slow motion" controls; do not duplicate Hold or Sustain. Retain a small quiet output spectrum. Selected chord is C major. Clearly separate pitch tuning from visualization time. No implementation jargon such as WebGPU or FFT in product controls.
Direction: HARMONIC OBSERVATORY. A precise, sensuous spectrum instrument with an expansive central harmonic spiral, not a generic solar system. Select "Overtones" in the top view switch.
Layout: slim 190px explorer rail left with a compact circle of fifths, C major selected, a row of scale notes and simple chord choices. Large central black canvas roughly 65% of the image width. Narrow 250px right inspector for the selected overtone pair. Keep panels visually quiet and mostly borderless. Large elegant "C major" title and three colored note chips near top of canvas.
Hero: a wide, near-front-facing logarithmic pitch spiral with four thin gray turns, one turn per octave, arranged like a precision scientific instrument. Roughly 24–36 discrete bright partial markers in cyan, coral and violet, sized by amplitude, lie precisely on the spiral. Fine colored filaments connect only meaningful near-coincidences. Two especially close partials are enlarged in a small elegant magnifier connected to the selected pair. Restrained glow on active markers, sharp cores and generous true-black negative space; no particulate cloud. Small octave ticks and a few readable labels make the mapping understandable. The image should feel luminous, richly structured and mesmerizing without becoming spaghetti.
Right inspector verbatim text: "Overtone pair", "C3 × 5", "654.1 Hz", "E3 × 4", "659.3 Hz", "Beating", "5.2 Hz", "Tune E3", a precise cents slider at "0.0 ct", and a small button "Align partials". Include a tiny slow beat-envelope drawing with cyan and coral traces. One understated instruction: "Drag a note to hear the alignment." The meaningful differences should be immediately legible.
This is a future design concept, not a claim that this is measured output. Render as an exceptionally polished shippable product mockup with actual musical content.

Clearly separate pitch tuning from visualization time. No implementation jargon such as WebGPU or FFT in product controls.
Direction: TUNING TERRAIN. An immersive, tactile instrument for exploring tuning with a continuous 3D mathematical landscape. Select "Tuning" in the top view switch. This composition should be visibly different from the reference and from a spiral visualization.
Layout: remove the permanent left sidebar to allow an expansive full-width plot above the keyboard. At top left of canvas an elegant "C major" and "Root C3" with a compact root selector. Put a small circle-of-fifths popover button nearby, not a whole big wheel. At the right edge place one carefully sized inspector about 250px wide with E3 and G3 tuning controls. Below the plot is one narrow horizontal comparison strip, then the shared sound toolbar and keyboard.
Hero: an exquisite precise topographic mathematical surface on a completely black background, seen from a gentle isometric angle. It has clear basins, ridges and saddles made from hundreds of fine gray contour lines and a sparse underlying mesh. A few restrained luminous cyan-to-coral-to-violet contour sections trace selected tuning routes; the whole surface is not a rainbow or glowing blob. The surface occupies most of the central 2/3 of the interface. Three or four tiny pitch-ratio markers help orient it. A bright cyan draggable dot sits in a local valley, with a fine coral comparison ghost dot nearby connected by a short path. The design feels like a beautifully engineered landscape you can actually play, not a fantasy mountain scene. No water, rocks, skies or stars.
Axis labels must read "E3 tuning" and "G3 tuning". Small legend reads "Estimated roughness" with "Lower" and "Higher"; do not label this a harmony score. Inspector text: "Tune this chord", "E3", "−13.7 ct", "G3", "+2.0 ct", "Equal", "Just", "Reset tuning". Comparison strip has "Equal temperament" and "Just intonation" with two small readable tuning silhouettes, plus one simple "Compare" button. One understated hint on the canvas: "Drag to explore nearby tunings."
Keep the color in the plot and selected piano notes. The UI controls remain neutral and elegant. Make it visually ambitious while remaining a plausible usable browser music tool.

Direction: CHORD ATLAS. A luxurious, spatial musical composition instrument built around a playable Tonnetz lattice and common-tone voice leading. Select "Chords" in the view switch. This should feel useful for discovering progressions and completely distinct from the spectrum spiral or a waveform plot.
Layout: very large nearly flat 2D lattice fills the main central-left workspace; a thin left edge only contains a compact key selector "C major" and modes "Explore / Progression". A generous right-side column around 280px contains the selected chord transformation and a short progression. Main canvas title "C major" with a subtle subtitle "Move one note. Hear a new chord." Retain black and grayscale chrome, the shared lower sound toolbar and playable piano.
Hero: a sophisticated spacious triangular Tonnetz lattice with quiet thin charcoal edges and readable pitch labels at small circular nodes. Mathematically meaningful neighbors: along one row label "F C G D A E", with the shifted row above "A E B F♯ C♯ G♯" and the shifted row below "D♭ A♭ E♭ B♭ F C". Avoid random repeated word soup. The selected C–E–G triangle is large, with very subtly tinted translucent interior and luminous narrow edges: C is cyan, E coral, G violet. The neighboring C–E♭–G triangle is a faint ghost sharing the C–G edge. Show a clean curved coral gesture from E toward E♭, while C and G remain strongly anchored. Only these two triangles are emphasized; inactive lattice fades gracefully into black at the edges. This is not a web of random neon nodes.
Right inspector exact text: "C → Cm", "2 shared notes", "E → E♭", "−1 semitone". A clear small button "Hear the change". Below: "Progression" with four quiet chord tiles "C", "Am", "F", "G", connected in order by a thin line. Below that a little piano-roll-like three-line voice-leading diagram with two straight shared-note lines and one stepping downward. Do not invent scores, approval marks, or percentages.
One lower canvas strip offers "Common tones", "Voice paths", and "Octave view". Keep spectrum subtle. Beautiful precise optical alignment and generous whitespace, unmistakably a professional instrument for musical exploration, never an educational worksheet or game map.
